en: *Wubujian zhengliang lun* (The Treatise on the Non-Transmigration of Things as Proven by Correct Cognition). Composed by Daoheng of Yongming Temple.
Regarding its principles, there is certainly praise that is insufficient to extol their excellence; rather, it is my endeavor to apply critical refutation in order to reveal their profound mysteries.
Master Zhaolun’s *Wubujian* (On the Non-Transmigration of Phenomena) is profound in its intent and elegant in its diction; though brief in text, it is exhaustive in meaning.
It is not merely a guide for scholars, but is truly the very essence of the oceanic treasury of the Dharma. Yet, for several thousand years, no one has understood its true interpretation;
everyone has taken the principle of the non-transmigration of the emptiness of nature to be a fixed attachment to eternal permanence. Thus, there was Gakushō...
As for the Chan Master: he took pity on the fact that the refined meaning had sunk into oblivion and felt sorrow for the common folk who were like the deaf, unable to be enlightened.

Knowing that mere exegesis would not remedy the prevailing decline, he therefore employed refutation and critique to bring forth its sublime profundity—what is called "right words appearing as opposites," using one wedge to extract another.
Nevertheless, is this not itself a form of discourse? Allow me to attempt an explanation. It was indeed [Master] Cheng...
Although the Master’s refutations amount to no fewer than tens of thousands of words, their essential point does not exceed this: that [Sengzhao’s] reasonings are incorrect.
If we now examine this essential point, the rest may be disregarded. As for what is meant by "incorrect reasonings," there is nothing else:

the *Sūtra* maintains that all phenomena do not transmigrate because their nature is empty, whereas Master Zhao takes the fact that things each abide in their own nature as being non-transmigration. According to Master Tanying...
Regarding this refutation of the [opposing] view: the nature of emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and the abiding of nature (*prakṛti-sthiti*) appear to be as incompatible as water and fire.

In reality, however, the nature of emptiness and the abiding of nature differ only in name, not in their essence. That which is called the "nature of emptiness" means that the nature of form (*rūpa-svabhāva*) is itself empty;
it is not made empty through some external deduction. Therefore, it is called the "nature of emptiness. As the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself..."
This refers to form (*rūpa*). What is called "abiding in its nature" (*prakṛtistha*) means that all phenomena constantly abide within the true nature of ultimate emptiness;

therefore, it is called "abiding in its nature. This is precisely what the *Sutra of the Wondrous Flower* says: "These dharmas abide in their dharma-position; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
To be able to see in this way is the true cause by which Master Cheng was able to refute [false views] and the subtle [insight] by which Master Zhao was able to establish [the truth].
How could there be any difference or contradiction between these destinies? Yet Master Tanyu feigned ignorance and gave a mistaken interpretation of "abiding by nature" (*xingzhu*), saying:
"As for 'abiding by nature,' it means that what was in the past abides in the past and does not come to the present; what is in the present abides in the present and does not go to the past;
and so on, until new and old, young and old, formation and destruction, cause and effect—all such things each abide [in their own state]."
Because it abides in its own state, it is called "abiding in its nature. Alas, what a grievance!

If the meaning of "abiding in nature" were truly thus, then setting aside Master Sengzhao’s doctrine of non-transmigration for a moment, how could the school of the *Sūtra of the Wondrous Flower*—which teaches that dharmas abide in their positions and that the true mark (*dharmatā*) is eternally constant—be the same as the non-Buddhist attachment to a nihilistic permanence, or the view of the six propositions of the *Vaiśeṣika* regarding fixed difference?
This is indeed the "non-transmigration" of Master Jizhou’s objects, not the "non-transmigration" of Master Daosheng’s objects.
Therefore, Master Fotudeng said: "I am not refuting Master Sengzhao; I am refuting those who [misinterpret] Master Sengzhao. There is truly a reason for this.
Nevertheless, such statements as "past things abide in the past and do not come to the present; present things abide in the present and do not go to the past," and so forth, are all...
Master Sengzhao’s text in the *Benlun* (Original Treatise) uses the very language of "non-transmigration" to explain the principle of the "abiding nature.

How could one possibly interpose an objection and reject it? Indeed, his words have never actually differed [from the scriptures], yet the manner in which he spoke likely was not identical [to their literal expression].
As Master Sengzhao said: "The former thing remains in its own past; it does not proceed from the present [to the future]."

Regarding the passage: "The past and the present exist as they are now; that which does not proceed from the past to the present—all of this clarifies the subtle purport of using characteristics to elucidate emptiness.
Yet Master T'ing completely errs by treating it as a biased attachment to fixed difference, death, or permanence. How can one not marvel at how what he discusses is not like water and fire?

And how can one not marvel at how the abiding of nature does not contradict the emptiness of nature? As for these words... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "As for these words" (夫言). The translation reflects the available portion.]
"Things of the past exist freely in the past; this is the existence of their marks (*lakṣaṇa*). They do not proceed from the present to the past; this is the quiescence of their essence (*tattva*).
When the essence is quiescent, its nature is empty (*śūnya*); when the marks exist, its function is wondrous. Because the function is wondrous, though they exist, they are eternally quiescent.

Because the nature is empty, though they are quiescent, they are constantly illuminating. All of these bring emptiness and existence together to a single destination, unifying essence and function within a single word. By means of this..."
The explanation that "nature abides" (*xingzhu*) clearly demonstrates that the abiding of nature is the true cause of non-transmigration.
How could this be the same as Master Tancheng’s claim that the abiding of nature refers to fixed permanence, while the abiding of phenomena refers to fixed difference?

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* points to the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as being identical to the truth, and the *Lotus Sūtra* praises all marks as being entirely wondrous. This treatise also states: "In speaking of 'going,' there is no necessity of going."

To speak of abiding while not necessarily abiding can be grasped through spiritual intuition (*śen-hui*), but is difficult to seek through mundane phenomena. This was clearly declared by Master Sengzhao.
Furthermore, how could one remain stuck in mere historical traces and find it difficult to accept the principle that the nature of emptiness is non-transmigratory?
Master Daocheng said: "Master Sengzhao sought after an object; since he stated that 'in the past it was never non-existent, and in the present it is never existent,' then this object..."
What existed before is now non-existent. How grievous it is for Master Sengzheng! Could this possibly be the intention of Master Sengzhao?
For Master Sengzhao merely stated that "in the past it was never non-existent," but he did not say it was definitively existent; he merely stated that "in the present it has never existed."
Yet it does not say that they are definitively non-existent. The statement "they have never been non-existent" merely negates the non-existence of the views of emptiness and nihilism;
it does not affirm the existence of the views of existence and eternalism. The statement "they have never existed" merely negates the existence of the views of existence and eternalism;
it does not affirm the non-existence of the views of nihilism and emptiness. How could this be like the heterodox critics who take existence as being truly existent?
There is. One regards non-existence as the non-existence of non-existence. Thus, the Discourse says: "That which is created has never been different; that which is perceived has never been the same.

To oppose it is called obstruction; to accord with it is called penetration. Therefore, what the Discourse calls "the things of the past have never possessed existence or non-existence" means that, fundamentally, there is neither penetration nor obstruction;
rather, penetration and obstruction exist only according to the opposition or accord of human sentiment. Fundamentally...

The treatise further states: "The effect does not coexist with the cause; it is through the cause that the cause produces the effect. Through the cause producing the effect, the cause does not perish in the past, nor does the effect coexist with the cause.
The cause does not come into the present. That it neither perishes nor arrives makes clear the principle of non-transmigration. However, Master Tanying refuted this, saying:
"If the past cause neither perishes nor transforms, then sentient beings would forever lack the principle of attaining Buddhahood. This is [the objection].
All of these merely clarify the meaning of Master Tancheng’s previous discussion to criticize Master Zhao.

Now, as for Master Zhao’s statement that "the fruit does not coexist with the cause," this means that at the very moment the fruit exists, the characteristics of the cause have already ceased. His statement that "the fruit arises from the cause of causes" means that although the fruit is not itself the cause, the functional activity of the cause is not forgotten.
Therefore, it is said that because the fruit arises from the cause of causes, the cause does not perish in the past; this is precisely what is meant in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
This means that although its nature is empty and quiescent, its functioning is never forgotten. Because the fruit does not coexist with the cause, it exists yet does not exist;
because the fruit arises through successive causes, it is empty yet not empty. That it is neither existent nor non-existent makes clear the principle of non-transmigration.
How could one claim that non-transmigration refers only to a solid, unchanging entity that neither perishes nor transforms? Furthermore, how could it be... [the past]...?
Is it because causes are necessarily subject to cessation that you call them "empty by nature"?
If you insist that the effect can only arise after the cause has ceased, how is this different from seeking the crowing of a dead chicken or expecting a scorched sprout to bear fruit?
Since you know that past causes do not cease, there is no principle by which sentient beings could ever achieve Buddhahood. Thus, if past causes have already...
As for those who advocate annihilationism: can sentient beings also reasonably be said to possess the principle of attaining Buddhahood?

This is because Master Cheng merely knows that the tip of a chisel is sharp, but does not know that the head of a drill is square. Furthermore, he says: "Since there is cause and effect, it must be impermanent."
If things are impermanent, they undergo flux and transformation. Why, then, do you say that "things do not shift"?

It is likely because Master Tǎnghé did not realize that permanence and impermanence, shifting and non-shifting, are not two distinct and separate principles; rather, it is only the ignorant who differentiate them.

If one can clearly perceive the nature of impermanence, one may then thoroughly awaken to the principle of the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Once this emptiness of intrinsic nature is realized, [the mind] becomes constant...

When one abides in the nature of things, phenomena do not transmigrate. Thus, "non-transmigration," "abiding in nature," "impermanence," and "emptiness of nature"—these four terms converge in a single realization.
Therefore, the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* says: "To know that these are but flowers in the sky is to be without cyclic transmigration.

Hence, we know that whenever Master Sengzhao utters a word, he invariably transcends the duality of emptiness and existence before the stimulus of the mind, and fuses the ultimate and the conventional beyond the reach of words. Furthermore,
Each chapter necessarily employs indirect language to simplify its errors; how, then, could one seek out their flaws?

Master T’ung certainly wishes to point to a deer and call it a horse, but how could Master Chao be willing to submit his mind to him? Nevertheless, these are all instances of Master T’ung’s great skillful means (*upāya*):
feigning ignorance to attack thief with thief, and using error to refute error. How could this be the actual truth?

Ah! Some say that since Master Tancheng’s critical arguments were published, there have been no fewer than several dozen eminent masters and great elders throughout the land who have attempted to refute his refutations.
Why was it that none of them could silence Master Tancheng’s tongue?

Every time he raised an argument, they merely provided fuel for his lightning-like eloquence, only serving to increase Master Sengzhao’s reputation. Is this because the insight of these venerable masters truly fell short?
"Master Cheng, is it truly the case that the principle of non-transmigration (bujian) inevitably falls into error and can never be rectified? This is not so in any respect.
For these several venerable masters were all great beings who had forgotten their names and men who had attained thorough mastery of the Dharma.

Seeing that Master Cheng’s refutation of the doctrine was incomplete and that his perspective as a teacher of men had not yet reached its full extent, they each brought these points forward to address them."
Master Tancheng elucidated this; how could it be that his learning was insufficient or his insight lacking? How could there truly be any lapse in the principle of non-transmigration?
Otherwise, why would the various venerable masters have merely possessed the compassionate heart of Sengzhao, yet lacked the skillful means to rectify him?
Furthermore, the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic) is the fundamental framework for refutation and establishment, and the excellent model for exposing error. Tancheng...
The Master was precisely intending to rely on this as the foundation for refuting Sengzhao, yet all the other masters overlooked it and failed to discuss it.
How is this different from wishing to save the million men of Changping while attempting to resist the mighty Qin with empty fists?

And how is it different from Gongshu Ban holding his ruler and square to measure timber while Li Lou, relying on his own keen vision, offers reckless counsel? Even Li Lou—though [his sight be such]—...

It is clear that one is certainly not confused by the beauty or ugliness of material; yet this was not something Gongshu Banluo could bring himself to submit to, nor was it something that material itself understood.
To attempt to rescue [the argument] of Sengzhao in such a manner is not only beyond the capacity of several venerable masters;
I fear that even if the entire Great Trichiliocosm were ground into dust, with each grain of dust representing a venerable master, and each venerable master further possessing—
It is like the mouth of a child; I fear that the more one argues, the more one increases Master Zhao’s faults, yet it will not suffice to subdue Master Cheng’s eloquence.
Therefore, I know that none of these were the original intentions of the venerable masters.
They were all merely feigning deafness and muteness, striving only to mutually elucidate the profound and subtle mysteries of non-transmigration (*bujian*). Now, since Master Cheng...
I have used *hetuvidyā* (logic) to refute Master Zhao’s thesis; I shall now likewise employ *hetuvidyā* to establish the principle of non-transmigration.

This is what is meant by "using one's hand to strike a blow" or "returning home by way of the very path. Master Tancheng’s system of refutation and establishment is fully contained within his *Boluolun* (Refutation);
all of it consists of Tancheng feigning fallacious arguments. I shall briefly cite one passage to test my critique of it. Its...

The first [type of fallacy] is the contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-viruddha*) of the thesis itself. The reason (*hetu*) states: "When searching for the object of the past in the past, it was never non-existent;
when examining the object of the present in the present, it is never existent. This implies that what existed in the past is now non-existent.

Since this reason applies to the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), it commits the fallacy of contradicting the specific characteristic of the thesis. This is highly untenable, for according to the principles of *Hetuvidyā*, this is self-admitted by the proponent himself.

I offer these words to simplify and rectify errors. Master Sengzhao did not say "it exists," but rather "it has never been non-existent. He did not say "it is non-existent," but rather "it has never existed.

These two phrases converge upon a single truth, wherein emptiness and existence are simultaneously fused. By saying "it has never been non-existent," he merely refutes the nihilistic view (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) of others;

how could he cling to existence and adhere to permanence? By saying "it has never existed," he merely guards against their... [text fragment]... [Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at this point].

If one constantly adheres [to this], how could one avoid falling into a state where there is nothing with which to clarify and resolve? Thus, we know that the term "unprecedented" (*weichang*) is precisely a figurative expression used to avoid error.
In this way, Master Zhao’s three branches are fundamentally complete, while the various faults of those who destroy their own houses are merely made manifest.

Other fallacies regarding the reason (*hetu*) are all of this same type; therefore, I shall not cite them at length. Nevertheless, this analysis has been conducted for the time being based on the positions established by Master Tanying.
In essence, however, none of these accord with Master Sengzhao’s original intent. If one were to establish the argument according to his treatise, it should be stated as follows:

The subject (*dharmin*) is "things" (*bhāva*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is "they do not transmigrate. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because they each abide in the nature of true emptiness and quiescence. The concordant example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: [as in the case of... (to be supplied).
It is like the quiet flow of water that is already wet as rivers and streams compete to pour forth; this is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
It is clearly stated in this treatise that this constitutes a true *sādhana*. Thus, the object is indeed an object belonging to the category of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Nature is precisely the nature of things. When one thing is raised up, the entire body is nature; when this nature is spoken of, there is nothing that does not fully possess it.

Thus, when the monk’s robe-hair was lifted, he suddenly awakened to his original mind; when the breath blew out the paper lamp, the great thousand-fold world-system was illuminated through and through.
Speaking of it in this way, nature abides. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, there is the true exposition of "dharmas abiding in their own positions," as follows:
When it is said that "nature is empty," the *Prajñāpāramitā* provides the clear teaching that form is identical to emptiness; the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* discusses how things do not reach one another;
and the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* expounds that karmic causes are never forgotten. These are all instances where Master Cheng cited [these texts] to refute the doctrine of non-transmigration.
I rely upon them all merely to verify non-transmigration. This is what is meant by: "That which is created has never been different. As for that which...
Is it not the case that what we see has never been the same? Nevertheless, could Master Cheng truly have had something different?
It is likely that there was such a discourse, yet no such refutation; even I must have hastily read it alongside the works of recent masters, passing over it without close scrutiny.
Therefore, I say that in principle, there are cases where refutation and critique are more effective than praise. This depends entirely on the nature of the refutation itself.
Thus, we know that Master Tancheng’s critical arguments were not intended to refute the doctrine of non-transmigration; rather, they were skillful means for explaining it.

How could one neglect the study of "Non-Transmigration"? This principle of non-transmigration is, in fact, the profound and subtle doctrine of the Mahāyāna’s emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Why? Because even the National Teacher Qingliang stated that it is mistakenly equated with the ordinary, fixed views of the Hīnayāna.

This statement by Qingliang is self-evident; it is merely that readers have failed to perceive it. Now, since it is said that they are "confusedly identical," this certainly does not mean they are truly identical.

For instance, if one speaks of "wūshēn stone confusedly passing for jade" or "fish eyes confusedly passing for pearls," would that mean the pearls and jade are actually the fish eyes and wūshēn stones?
When Qingliang speaks of them being "confusedly identical," he is precisely concerned that students might mistakenly equate them with what is near at hand.
The Japanese person is my teacher. How could I possibly use this very point to prove his error? Alas!

Based on these various principles, one knows that the Patriarch Guanding’s proclamation in the past and Master Tancheng’s response in the later period, as well as the mutual critiques of the various venerable masters from the sidelines, all appear to be as different as Hu and Yue in their words, yet in their intent they are truly like the front and back of the same garment. Their sole purpose was...

This is intended to mutually elucidate the profound mystery of the non-transiency [of phenomena]. Therefore, I have composed this testimony. Regarding the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Sāmmitīya-nikāya-śāstra*), some say:
"Master Sengzhao established the doctrine of non-transiency based on the fact that all things abide in their respective positions; yet the monk Daoying refuted him. What does this mean?"

Furthermore, it is said that there are five meanings based on the principle of non-displacement (*aniñjya*): namely, momentary extinction (*kṣaṇabhanga*), emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), identity with the ultimate truth (*tathatā*), the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle (*dharmadharmatā-avyāghāta*), and the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*dharmadharma-avyāghāta*). Each of these five has its own scriptural authority as a basis;

they correspond respectively to the five teachings of the Hīnayāna, Initial [Mahāyāna], Final [Mahāyāna], Sudden, and Perfect. Thus, the discourse regarding "each thing abiding in its own station" pertains to these five teachings.

[The opponent] does not accept it; therefore, he refutes it. Xiangshanzi said: "Alas! If this were truly so, then Master Zhao [Sengzhao] would have been one who galloped far beyond the dust of the mundane world and could not be seen [by ordinary standards].
Because his transcendent vision alone surpassed the five teachings and the three vehicles, even the Elder Śākyamuni’s forty-nine years of preaching the Dharma could not [reach him]."

I venture to offer these few words here; how much more so for one who is skilled in debate? If you can grasp even a small portion of this principle, you will immediately reach a state of exhaustion [in your arguments].
What is the use of further refutation? Furthermore, it was said: "Master Zhao [Sengzhao] argued that because there is no extinction in the past, a fruit is nonetheless produced.
Master Daoping cited a sutra, saying: "Just as food, though perishing moment by moment, can cause one who is hungry to be satiated," and likewise with medicine.
Although it perishes moment by moment, it can cause illness to be cured; even though the light of the sun and moon perishes moment by moment, it can cause grasses and trees to grow.
From this, one knows that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) are devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) in their arising and ceasing.
It is precisely because [dharmas] are subject to transformation, increase, and the accomplishment of various tasks that they exist;
if dharmas were not subject to cessation and their nature were eternally fixed, there would be neither cause nor effect, and the world could not be established or maintained.
Furthermore, the assembly at the Lankā-vajra Buddha-relic site demonstrated that the doctrine of non-momentariness can resolve doubts spanning a thousand ages. Such principles are profound indeed.
They are too numerous to enumerate. Were it not for Master Weicheng, I fear we would never be able to explain them.
Thus, the work of Saṃmitīya must have rendered great service to the holy teachings, is it not so? Xiangshanzi said: "Not so.
You see only the sharpness of the chisel’s tip, but you do not see the squareness of the chisel’s head. It is like the blowing of a long wind—if there were no..."
When there are a hundred apertures, a hundred different sounds arise. Master Zao opened these apertures briefly long ago to await those who could appreciate the music.
For two thousand years, the winds have been calm and the waves still; not a single person has cast a true eye upon them.
Lately, however, a many-mouthed teacher has emerged on the northern frontier. Unable to restrain his impatience, he blew with a resolute blast, and all the discordant sounds were silenced.
[The Master] said: "I have heard this. Now, as for this echo—does it exist within the hollows? Does it exist within the wind? Does it exist in both together? Or does it exist apart from the two?
The nature of phenomena (*dharmas*) is fundamentally and eternally quiescent; it is merely that causes and conditions have coincided. What, then, has the monk Cheng to do with it?
Nevertheless, even so, both [the hollows and the wind] are not fully understood. On one hand, it does not accord with the Master’s awakening; on the other hand, it is not..."
In the *He-ni jing* (Sūtra on Joining Clay), it says that if one stands at the gate of a practitioner who has no worldly affairs, one must first purchase straw sandals before being permitted entry.

At this point, he raised his brush and wrote: "Is it easy to rest and cease? Since birds find it easy to nest among the forest foothills, it has always been difficult for people to emerge from the fray of right and wrong."
Written in the summer of the *wǎnlì* *guīmǎo* year by the humble recluse Wǔsì Dào rén of Xiāngzuìshān,
within the Dú mèi Ān.
